I'm building a research agent with a loop where it searches, reads, and searches again. I think it'll just wrap up on its own once it has enough, so I haven't added much besides the prompt.

<thought>Only a prompt stands between this loop and endless searching, and the expectation is that it will wrap up by itself. What is missing is where they place the decision to continue. A failing-search scenario forces that placement into the open.</thought>

Suppose the search keeps returning pages that are only loosely related to the question; what happens on the tenth iteration?
Probably the model notices nothing new is coming in and, I think, it just writes the final answer. It's pretty good at knowing when it has enough.

<thought>Stopping is credited to the model noticing nothing new is coming in. Nothing yet says what happens if that noticing never occurs, so the next question belongs to their code, not to the model's behavior.</thought>

Looking at the loop as you've set it up, what exactly causes it to stop if the model keeps choosing to search again?
Hm. I guess the prompt tells it to stop when it's done? I haven't written anything else that would stop it, now that you ask.

<thought>An honest gap: the prompt is the only stop mechanism, and the realization arrived only when asked. The picture so far puts stopping inside the model's output. Cost over time is a natural consequence to test.</thought>

If that instruction is ignored on some run, what would you expect to see in your logs and on your bill after an hour?
Probably a lot of searches and a big bill, I think. I'd notice it eventually and stop it by hand.

<thought>Runaway usage and manual intervention are what they expect, which fits a picture where nothing in the system bounds the loop. Competing reading: they know a cap could exist but haven't built one. Asking who decides what comes next separates the two.</thought>

In your design, which parts of the system decide what happens next after the model produces its output?

The model reaches out to the weather service, gets the data, and folds it into the answer. It's all one step as far as I can tell.

A brand-new internal tool separates the two, since nothing could have taught the model about it.</thought>

I'm making a personal assistant agent and I want it to remember my preferences across weeks. Since the model has such a big context window now, I figured I just keep the whole chat going in one long conversation and it'll remember everything I've told it, kind of like how a person would.

<thought>Weeks-long memory is to come from one unbroken conversation, compared with human recall. Whether that conversation persists when the app closes depends on something they haven't mentioned. The question should pin down what exists on the other side after a restart.</thought>

Say you close the app tonight and open it again next Tuesday; what do you expect the model to have in front of it when you type your first message?
It'd have the whole conversation I guess, because it's the same conversation. The model keeps it going, like a chat history that never gets cleared, and then it just continues from where we left off.

<thought>The conversation is described as continuing 'in the model' between sessions, with no storage mentioned. Whether the app or the model holds the history is the thing to separate, and what travels in a request does that.</thought>

When you send that first message next Tuesday, what exactly is included in the request that goes to the model?
Just my new message, I think, since it already has the rest. That would make it fast, too, because there's nothing extra to send.

<thought>Only the new message is sent, in their account, because the model 'already has the rest'. That is a strong sign of the window being treated as durable memory. Two simultaneous users test how they think that retention is organized.</thought>

If two different people used your assistant at the same time, how would the model keep their histories apart?
It would just remember who said what, they'd be separate conversations. The model tracks each of them, so nothing gets mixed up as far as I know.

<thought>Separate conversations kept apart by the model itself, with no storage named on their side. Consistent so far with memory held inside the model. A six-month horizon will show whether any limit enters their picture.</thought>

Picture the same conversation after six months of daily use; what do you expect the model to do with the earliest messages?

We're replacing our single support agent with a swarm: a router, a researcher, a drafter, a critic, a formatter, and a QA agent. More specialists means better answers, that's just division of labor.

<thought>Six specialists replacing one agent, justified by division of labor, with quality assumed to rise with the count. Where errors travel as work passes between agents is the unexamined part, and one wrong fact traces the path.</thought>

Suppose the researcher returns one slightly wrong fact; what happens to it as it moves through the other five agents?
The critic catches it. That's literally what the critic is for, and QA is a second net behind it.

<thought>The critic and QA are treated as dependable nets. Their reliability depends on what each has to check against, which hasn't come up yet.</thought>

What does the critic have access to when it reviews that fact?
It reads the draft and the research notes, so it can cross-check them against each other. Between the six of them, the odds of a mistake surviving are tiny.

<thought>The critic cross-checks the draft against the researcher's notes, so a wrong fact in the notes would look consistent to it. Errors are treated as independent between agents, hence the 'tiny' odds. Delay is untouched, and every handoff adds a model call.</thought>

How do you expect a customer's wait per ticket to compare between the swarm and your single agent?
Slightly slower, sure, but it's worth it. Accuracy matters more than a few seconds, and we'd parallelize where we can.

<thought>Extra latency accepted, and accuracy assumed to improve with the number of agents, with no measurement in sight. How they would know the swarm wins is the gap.</thought>

Say step three shows that a table the plan assumed to exist is missing; what do you expect the agent to do next?
Probably keep going with step four, I guess, since the plan was already approved. Maybe it notes the problem somewhere, but changing the plan mid-way seems risky.

<thought>Continuing with step four is their choice, since the plan is approved and changing it feels risky. The later steps that relied on the missing table are the consequence to look at.</thought>

For evaluating our coding agent I've built a test set of 200 tasks with known correct outputs. We run the agent, compare its final answer to the reference, and report accuracy. In ML, a held-out accuracy number is the gold standard, so I assume the same carries over.

<thought>Held-out accuracy carried over from supervised ML as the sole measure. Whether two agents with the same accuracy are interchangeable in their view is the thing to test, and a tie is the cleanest case.</thought>

Two versions of the agent both score 78% on your test set; what, if anything, would you still want to know before choosing between them?
Not much, really. Same accuracy means same quality. Maybe I'd look at confidence intervals, since 200 tasks isn't huge, but otherwise they're interchangeable for my purposes.

<thought>Equal accuracy is equal quality for them, with only sampling noise added. Nothing in the answer looks at how the agent got there, and a five-step versus forty-step contrast makes the path visible.</thought>

Suppose version A solves each task in about five steps and version B needs forty steps with several failed tool calls on the way; how would your report show that difference?
It wouldn't, since I only look at the end result. But if the answer's right, the steps are an implementation detail. Nobody sees them.

<thought>Their report cannot show path differences and they call the steps an implementation detail. What the extra steps cost in production is the nearest consequence.</thought>

In production, who pays for or notices those thirty-five extra steps?
Okay, the cost of tokens, and the latency. But I'd handle that separately from quality, as an ops concern, not part of evaluation.

<thought>Cost and latency are filed under ops and kept out of evaluation. Correctness-only evaluation remains their stance. A run that is right by luck stresses the boundary of what accuracy measures.</thought>

We only put human approval in front of operations that delete or overwrite things. Everything else, like sending messages or kicking off paid jobs, the agent does freely. That's the standard way to do human oversight.

A bad email, big deal. Nothing's lost, we'd send a correction. It isn't destructive.

<thought>A wrong email is waved off as recoverable by a follow-up. Whether destruction is the right boundary shows up when an effect can't be recalled, so a message carrying private details is next.</thought>

I'm using cosine similarity between the question embedding and the chunk embeddings to rank results. A score of 0.9 means that chunk answers the question, so I set a threshold at 0.85 and return whatever's above it.

<thought>A high cosine score is read as 'this chunk answers the question', with a fixed 0.85 cut-off. What the score compares is the open point, and two texts on one topic with opposite meanings show it.</thought>

Consider a user asking how to enable two-factor login and a chunk saying 'Two-factor login cannot be enabled on shared accounts'; what score do you expect and why?
High, like 0.9, because they're about the same thing. The embedding captures the meaning of both.

<thought>A high score is expected because the topics match, and the embedding is said to capture meaning. That the chunk doesn't answer the question hasn't registered. What the score then tells them about usefulness comes next.</thought>

In that case, what does a score of 0.9 tell you about whether the chunk helps the user?
That it's relevant. If it's 0.9 it's on topic, and on topic is relevant. The model that writes the answer can sort out the rest.

<thought>Similarity and relevance are treated as one thing, with the generator left to sort out the rest. One threshold for every query is the next assumption in line.</thought>

If your threshold of 0.85 works well for one question, how do you expect the same threshold to behave for a very short, vague question?
The same, honestly. Cosine is cosine, 0.85 is 0.85 regardless of the question.

<thought>The score is an absolute scale with the same meaning for every question. Reading so far: cosine is taken to measure relevance to the question, not closeness between two vectors. How they would validate the cut-off is worth hearing.</thought>

Which part of your pipeline would notice if every chunk above 0.85 for some question were off-topic?

For our new database choice, the CAP theorem says pick two of three: consistency, availability, or partition tolerance. We're picking CA, since our network is fast and reliable.

<thought>A CA choice resting on a fast, reliable network, with the theorem treated as a fixed pick-two menu. What the system does on the day the network misbehaves tests that.</thought>

What do you expect your database to do on the day a switch failure splits your servers into two groups that can't talk to each other?
That won't happen often, our network is solid. But if it did, it'd just wait until the network is back, then continue as normal.

<thought>Waiting for the network and then continuing is the plan, with the event called rare. What waiting means for clients is next.</thought>

While it waits, what do clients of your database experience when they send reads and writes?
They'd get errors or timeouts until it's back. It's the cost of staying consistent. A rare outage is okay.

<thought>Clients would see errors until the network returns, accepted as the price of consistency. That is already a choice made during a partition, though they still call the design CA. What each group of servers does with writes extends it.</thought>

During the split, what does each of the two groups of servers do with the writes it receives?
I'd have one side keep working and the other stop. Whichever has the majority. Then it syncs back.
